lesson.text: Quick memory: what is a mentor? (Someone who teaches you.) Today: networks, your good name and staying safe online.
A network is the people you know and who know you. The strongest have all kinds of people: older, younger, from other places.
Scientists found that friendships across different groups are among the strongest links to getting ahead in life.
Your good name grows when you keep your word, and when you tell the truth early if you can't.
Keep in touch: a thank-you or a hello when you don't need anything keeps a connection warm.
Online, only friends a grown-up approved. Never share your address, your school or a password: tell a grown-up.
Try it in the practice village: connect Mei, Ana, Rosa, Gemma and Kenji.

choices: all kinds of people in it

exercises.prompt: A stranger online asking for your address is fine.
exercises.explain: False: don't reply, and tell a grown-up.

exercises.prompt: A friend asks for your password. You...
choices: never share it, and tell a grown-up

matches: Gemma, who knows the clay pit
exercises.explain: Mei and Ana, Rosa and Gemma, Kenji and Rosa.

exercises.prompt: You can't keep a promise. To protect your good name...
choices: tell them early, say sorry, offer a new time
exercises.explain: Tell them early, say sorry, offer a new time.

exercises.prompt: Keeping in touch only when you need something makes a strong connection.
exercises.explain: False: keep in touch when you need nothing too.

exercises.prompt: Helping two people meet: put it in order.
items: find two people who can help each other
exercises.explain: Find them, introduce them, let them make their deal.
Approved friends and telling a grown-up are safe.

exercises.prompt: Your network: 4 family, 6 friends, 3 teachers and 2 neighbours. How many people?
Why are older people great to know?
choices: they know things nobody else knows
exercises.explain: They know things nobody else knows.
